questions.x: Magic methods like __construct(), __destruct(), __wakeup(), and __toString() are called by PHP automatically at defined moments. You never call them directly, they fire when their trigger condition is met.
questions.h: The double underscore prefix is a naming convention in PHP. What kind of functions does PHP call on your behalf, without you writing an explicit call?

o: When you call delete($obj) on the object
When the object goes out of scope and is garbage-collected by PHP
When the script encounters a fatal error
When you call $obj->destroy()
questions.x: PHP calls __destruct() automatically when an object's reference count drops to zero or when the script ends. In a deserialization exploit, an injected object's __destruct() runs at script end, executing attacker-controlled logic.
questions.h: The name des-truct hints at destruction. Objects are destroyed when they are no longer needed. When exactly does PHP decide an object is no longer needed?

o: When the object is first created with new
Immediately after unserialize() reconstructs the object
When the session is destroyed
When the object is converted to a string
questions.x: __wakeup() fires right after unserialize() finishes building the object. It is intended for post-deserialization initialization but can be used as a gadget if it contains dangerous operations.
questions.h: The method name is a metaphor: the object was 'sleeping' in its serialized form. When does it 'wake up'?

o: When you call intval() on the object
When the object is used in a string context, for example in echo or string concatenation
When you call serialize() on the object
When the object is used as an array key
questions.x: __toString() is invoked whenever PHP needs a string representation of the object: echo $obj, string concatenation, or passing it to a string function. If __toString() contains dangerous code, using the object as a string triggers it.
questions.h: The method name tells you the context. When does PHP need to convert an object to a string?

questions.q: Why are magic methods particularly useful in deserialization gadget chains?
o: They bypass PHP's type system entirely
They execute automatically without any explicit method call, so injecting an object via unserialize() is sufficient to trigger dangerous code
They are always public and cannot be made private
PHP optimizes magic methods to run before security checks
questions.x: An attacker does not need to call any method. Simply constructing the serialized string and passing it to unserialize() causes PHP to build the object. When the object is later destroyed, __destruct() fires. No explicit invocation needed.
questions.h: The attacker only controls the serialized input, not the code execution flow. How can they still trigger a specific method on an object they just deserialized?
